stories.summary: In office, Donald Trump asked the IRS and the FBI to investigate and torment his political rivals. By and large they refused, saying the requests were illegal and broke their rules. Trump also could not stop the Democrats from raising money, hiring advisors, holding rallies and getting out the vote in 2020. Even so, Biden only squeaked through, and because the court cases against Trump have not played out in time, he remains viable in 2024.
stories.insight: A populist's real limit is the culture inside the state's coercive arms. When career officials serve rules rather than rulers, the leader cannot capture them. The thin 2020 margin is the sobering coda: even with free speech, a working media and working intellectuals, institutions buy time but do not decide the outcome.
stories.quote: So he asked the IRS, the income tax department, and the FBI to go investigate and torment his rivals. And by and large, they refused to do so. Like, can you think about that? How marvelous is that?

stories.topic: The Richest Man Who Dared Oppose the President
stories.summary: Jeff Bezos, the richest person in the US, openly took an anti-Trump position. He also owned the Washington Post, which exposed the misdeeds of the Trump years. Ajay notes that rich people are usually the most timid, because they have the most to lose. Amit adds that under Bezos the Post kept running anti-Amazon and anti-Bezos stories.
stories.insight: Whether the rich feel safe enough to criticise the government is a barometer of a country's institutional quality. Amit's addition: strong institutions breed values that become part of the culture, strong enough that an owner cannot bend his own newsroom.
stories.quote: So in a way, rich people have hostages. They have the most to lose, and in a way, rich people could be the most timid, because you just don't want to mess with the government.

stories.summary: Ajay says up front that he is sympathetic to Israel. It came out of nothing and a war in 1948, and was built by European Jews who carried enormous human capital. As a sign of its liberal decency, he notes that gay people cross illegally from neighbouring Arab countries every day because homosexuality is legal in Israel. After the USSR fell, a large wave of Jewish immigrants arrived from Eastern Europe, notably Russia. They brought conservative values on religion, women and personal freedom, which opened the way for hardline religious-nationalist politics.
stories.insight: A democracy's character depends on the values its citizens carry, and large shifts in who those citizens are can reshape electoral politics within a generation. Even a great success story can slide back into fighting the demons of the twentieth century.
stories.quote: So there is a war for the soul of Israel that is afoot and it is alive and well.

stories.summary: Benjamin Netanyahu tried to give the executive veto power over the selection of judges. The public poured into the streets, and the movement was strikingly led by people from elite military formations. They said they had given blood for the country but would not let the executive ride roughshod over the judiciary. The protests won about 75%, though not 100%, of what they fought for.
stories.insight: Military people usually suffer most from strongman machismo and are often the first to back the destruction of institutions. Here they championed separation of powers, which reveals how deep Israel's liberal core runs.
stories.quote: look, we are soldiers, we have given our life and our blood to protect this country. But we do not believe that the executive branch should ride roughshod over the judicial branch.

stories.topic: Hungary: Von Neumann's Country Goes Thuggish
stories.summary: Hungary, the country of John von Neumann, was expected to flourish after communism, as Czechoslovakia did. Instead it became a thuggish right-wing state despite being in the EU and NATO. Elections still happen, but police go after the opposition, the press is gone, and fundraising and mobilising are impossible. The Central European University was driven out and relocated to a free country. Viktor Orbán has won five times.
stories.insight: Climbing out of a thuggish regime and building sound institutions is extremely hard. Even membership of Europe's civilising clubs does not guarantee it, and Ajay sees no sign yet of how Hungary's slide ends.
stories.quote: And for me, it was a reminder that it is very, very difficult to rise out of a thuggish regime, the communist regime, and create good institutions and create sound institutions.

stories.summary: Poland was invaded by Nazi Germany on 1 September 1939 and by Russia on 16 September 1939. After the war it was swallowed by the Russians, who installed a communist party. Stalin had a careful list drawn up of 40,000 members of the Polish elite, and they were murdered. Ajay asks listeners to imagine the same happening to any country they love.
stories.insight: Culture is transmitted by people. Killing a country's intellectual, business and cultural elite destroys its foundations, and it takes generations to rebuild that knowledge and those norms.
stories.quote: Imagine a carefully made list of the forty thousand people who make up the intellectual and the business and the cultural elite of the country. And imagine that they get murdered.

stories.topic: The EU as a Rough Working Draft
stories.summary: Around 2005, Ajay visited Poland and talked at length with the builders of the new post-1989 state. They told him the EU was their stabilising force: instead of designing every law and institution from scratch, they got a rough template from the EU. Poland and Ukraine started at similar levels after communism. Poland, inside the EU and NATO, took off; Ukraine, outside them and subject to constant Russian meddling, did not.
stories.insight: Institution-building is far easier when you can copy a working model and are anchored inside a stable club. External anchors act as ballast that carries a young democracy forward.
stories.quote: rough working draft from the EU of what a law roughly looks like, of what an institution roughly looks like.

stories.summary: Poland was the post-communist star pupil, then spent ten years under the Law and Justice Party (PiS). Ajay describes PiS as an alliance of farmers, Christians and thugs that opposed women's freedom, Western influence and foreigners, and monopolised power. Yet Poland's Freedom House score stayed at 80/100. In the October 2023 election, the centre-left party led by Donald Tusk won. Poland now faces the messy task of undoing institutional damage without itself breaking the rule of law.
stories.insight: Populism can be reversed, especially in a country that has not been hollowed out too far and is anchored in the EU and NATO. But the cure has to respect due process, which makes repair slow and difficult.
stories.quote: So you can't just send the police and grab the chief justice. Okay? You've got to do things in a way that respects the rule of law.

stories.summary: Ajay recalls spending three days visiting historical sites in Warsaw, weeping like a baby. Amit reflects that a tourist with no background sees only buildings, streets and weather, but the deeper you go, everything takes on meaning. Ajay sums it up: learning makes travel come alive; otherwise just go to the beach in Goa.
stories.insight: Knowing the history of a place turns sightseeing into an emotional encounter with human civilisation. The preparation is the travel.
stories.quote: The magic of travel is the child of learning culture, learning history. then travel comes alive.

stories.summary: Amit remembers downloading photographs over 90s dial-up: the image first appeared as a pixelated blur, then slowly sharpened into high definition, and the sharpening itself was thrilling. Learning what 'populism' really means felt the same way. A vague notion of 'popular' resolved into a clear frame for seeing the world.
stories.insight: Good concepts don't just add information; they bring a blurry picture of the world into focus. That moment of seeing clearly is one of the great pleasures of learning.
stories.quote: But then you read more and you discover these frames of seeing and I just find that that's so beautiful and miraculous that we can actually do that and make ourselves see better.

stories.topic: Why They Stayed Silent on Hamas and Israel
stories.summary: After the Hamas attacks and Israel's retaliation, many commenters asked the hosts to discuss it. They declined because they lacked enough knowledge. Amit still states his position: he is against Hamas, which he calls evil and the worst thing that happened to Palestine, and against the Israeli state as it currently is. He cares for the Palestinian people and sympathises with the Israeli people.
stories.insight: In a black-and-white discourse even a carefully nuanced position draws attacks from both sides. Knowing the limits of your knowledge, and saying so, is itself an intellectual virtue.
stories.quote: If you speak against Israel, it is assumed you are anti-Semitic, which is daft. If you speak against Hamas, it is assumed that you're against the Palestinian people, which is daft.

recommendations.creator: Jan-Werner Müller
recommendations.context: The backbone of the episode. Amit walks through Müller's seven traits of populists and three ways populists consolidate power, and names it again as his closing recommendation.
recommendations.reason: It taught Amit most of what he knows about populism. It replaces the naive 'populism = popular' with a precise checklist for spotting populists anywhere, which he says 'everyone should read.'

recommendations.item: Why Both Modi and Trump Are Textbook Populists
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit mentions he wrote a column on Müller's book 'a long time back' (2017), linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: An application of Müller's framework to contemporary politics, as a companion to the book.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2016 column on Trump, written before he read Müller, mentioned while discussing simplistic narratives.
recommendations.reason: It argues that Trump won a following by offering simple stories: jobs shipped overseas, immigrants taking jobs. These are simplistic and wrong, but they appear to explain the world. Amit reached Müller's 'simplistic narratives' point on his own.

recommendations.creator: George Orwell
recommendations.context: Amit's closing recommendation, alongside Animal Farm.
recommendations.reason: Amit says it will teach you so much about politics and calls it a masterpiece that feels like 'the future written in the past.'

recommendations.creator: George Orwell
recommendations.context: Recommended together with 1984 as Orwell's two great novels.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls both novels masterpieces that teach you a great deal about politics and the world.

recommendations.creator: George Orwell
recommendations.context: Amit notes he has recommended Orwell's essays on the show before.
recommendations.reason: He still has 'a softer corner' for the essays over the novels, calling Orwell 'a great genius, a great writer.'

recommendations.creator: William Golding
recommendations.context: Ajay's response to Amit's Orwell recommendations.
recommendations.reason: Ajay spent his life worrying about 1984, but feels we have stumbled into Lord of the Flies instead. The social media dystopia is people bullying and tormenting each other, and 'you don't even need the state to make you miserable.'

recommendations.creator: Timothy Snyder
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation of the week, which he says repeats one he has made before.
recommendations.reason: Ajay thinks it is important enough to recommend a second time in an episode about the populist threat to democracy.

recommendations.creator: Timothy Snyder and Nora Krug
recommendations.context: Set up with the Beauty and the Beast scene about a book with no pictures.
recommendations.reason: An illustrated version for readers who need pictures. Ajay says you should give one to 'every WhatsApp uncle in your life.'

recommendations.creator: Plato
recommendations.context: Ajay cites it while discussing why simplistic messages win in mass democracies.
recommendations.reason: Plato was clear-eyed about democracy's weaknesses long before radio, rallies, TV and social media made it easy to blast simplistic messages to the masses.

recommendations.creator: Timur Kuran
recommendations.context: Amit invokes Kuran's preference falsification and preference cascades when explaining what is new about the social media era.
recommendations.reason: It explains how hidden preferences can suddenly cascade into the open, a process social media now amplifies.

recommendations.creator: Freedom House
recommendations.context: Ajay uses its democracy scores to compare Poland (80/100), Israel (74/100) and Hungary (65/100) around October 2023.
recommendations.reason: A decent, easy-to-use democracy measure. Rival measures disagree somewhat but agree quite a bit.

recommendations.context: Mentioned as an alternative to Freedom House.
recommendations.reason: Ajay thinks V-Dem is in many ways the better measure of democracy, though more work to use.

recommendations.creator: Walt Disney
recommendations.context: The setup for Ajay's On Tyranny recommendation.
recommendations.reason: Its scene of the male character flipping through Belle's book, complaining it has no pictures, and Belle replying that some people can use their imagination.

recommendations.creator: Bee Gees
recommendations.context: Ajay quotes it to kick off the definition of populism.
recommendations.reason: 'It's only words and words are all we have' captures the episode's opening point: getting the technical meaning of words right is the foundation of clear thinking.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The episode's show notes say Amit's newsletter is 'furiously active again.'
recommendations.reason: Readers are invited to read and subscribe now that it is being published actively again.

recommendations.item: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit refers back to it on the interplay of money and power and on 'rational ignorance.'
recommendations.reason: It lays the groundwork for why voters fall for simplistic narratives and how populist clientelism differs from normal interest-group politics.

recommendations.item: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit cites it while admitting his own frustration with elites and how academia is broken.
recommendations.reason: It is the backdrop to Amit's point that elite complacency, entitlement and condescension are real problems, even though anti-elitism is dangerous.

recommendations.item: The Brave New Future of Electricity (Episode 40 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit contrasts it with this episode while disclaiming expertise in political science.
recommendations.reason: An episode where Ajay brought deep domain knowledge on energy and renewables, unlike this one, where both hosts approach populism as non-experts with skin in the game.

core_ideas.concept: Fields Hijack Common Words
core_ideas.explanation: Words like 'nationalism' and 'populism' mean something quite different to political scientists than to ordinary speakers. Populism is not 'what is popular'; it is toxic. Every field appropriates everyday English words, and if you read technical writing with the everyday meaning in mind, you will misunderstand it. Mastering a field's handful of core terms is half the battle.
core_ideas.quote: if you can correctly say market failure, if you can correctly say public good, if you can correctly say adverse selection, and if you can correctly say moral hazard, then basically you're an economist.

core_ideas.concept: Only Some of the People Are 'The People'
core_ideas.explanation: Müller's core insight is that populism is anti-pluralist. Populists define 'the people' as those who support them and treat everyone else as illegitimate. Trump said the other people don't matter and called the press 'the enemies of the people.' The same move appears when supporters are 'patriots' and critics are 'anti-national.'
core_ideas.quote: the core claim of populism is that only some of the people are the people.

core_ideas.concept: The Seven-Point Populist Playbook
core_ideas.explanation: Müller's checklist of what populists share: (1) defining the people as their supporters; (2) anti-elite rhetoric; (3) acting like victims, with majorities nursing invented historical grievances; (4) monolithic parties that turn into personality cults; (5) performed proximity to the people ('I worked in the mills'); (6) simplistic narratives; (7) conspiracy theories, which grow naturally out of the rest. Ajay urges listeners to keep it as a mental toolkit.
core_ideas.quote: majorities act like mistreated minorities.

core_ideas.concept: Politics Needs an Enemy
core_ideas.explanation: Carl Schmitt argued that having an enemy, an 'other', is essential to politics. If there is no external invader to rally against, populists manufacture internal enemies. They also pose as outsiders while being hardcore insiders: Amit points to Trump as a crony capitalist embedded in lobbying for forty years.
core_ideas.quote: what is essential to politics is having an enemy

core_ideas.concept: Simplistic Narratives and Rational Ignorance
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's favourite of Müller's seven points. The world is complex and we understand it through stories simpler than reality. Voters are 'rationally ignorant': they have livings to earn. So 'your jobs went overseas, immigrants took the rest' beats an honest, multifactorial explanation, and it supplies an 'other' to rail against. People with integrity stay with the nuanced truth; populists don't care. Ajay adds that hatred is the simplest narrative of all.
core_ideas.quote: it is so complex that simple stories are a feature, not a bug for the normal person.

core_ideas.concept: Great Leaders Bring Out Our Best; Populists Our Worst
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's test for a leader is which part of us they appeal to. Populists reduce us to our identity and fan resentment. Amit adds a grim mechanic: love and solidarity don't make people rush out to vote, but anger and hatred do.
core_ideas.quote: So I always think that great leaders make us better than who we are. They bring out the best in us. They ask of us that find the good inside you.

core_ideas.concept: Populism Cuts Across Left and Right
core_ideas.explanation: Hitler, Mao, Lenin and Trump were all populists, operating under very different systems, and both left and right populism are equally toxic. Neither the left/right binary nor democracy/totalitarianism classifies them correctly. Amit's preferred lens is consent versus coercion. By that lens, every Indian party is left on economics, right on social issues, and statist throughout.
core_ideas.quote: the frame that matters to me is freedom and authoritarianism, right? It is consent and coercion. That is a binary.

core_ideas.concept: The Populist Engine: Underclass Against the Elites
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's reading of the field is that the central engine of populism is rousing the underclass to hate the elite. He traces it through the French Revolution, Marx, Hitler, Lenin and Mao. A movement mobilises against the cultural, business and intellectual elites, captures the political elite (the state), and then destroys the other three, gutting the country's capability.
core_ideas.quote: a political movement seeks to stoke against them and ultimately command the state, the political elite, and put the knife into the other three.

core_ideas.concept: Rehabilitate 'Elite', but Elites Must Look in the Mirror
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that truth, beauty and wealth creation come from elites, and that treating 'elite' as a dirty word is populism of the left. Amit agrees that anti-elitism becomes anti-knowledge and anti-expertise, so leaders end up taking advice from quacks. He adds a corrective: elites are often complacent, entitled and condescending. When people vote against your values, the first job is introspection.
core_ideas.quote: even if the people vote in someone who does not align with your values, that doesn't mean something is wrong with the people. It means something is wrong with you and your message

core_ideas.concept: Tribes Over Principles
core_ideas.explanation: Within eight years Trump turned the Republican Party into the opposite of what it stood for. He became an enemy of free markets, with 2016 trade policies identical to Bernie Sanders'. Amit's disillusioning conclusion is that many people hold principles only because their tribe does, and switch when the tribe switches.
core_ideas.quote: a lot of people who claim to believe in principles are actually tribal. They claim to believe in principles because their tribe does so. But if the tribe changes its principles, they'll go along with that.

core_ideas.concept: Parties Need to Be Institutions Too
core_ideas.explanation: Political theory says the state should be depersonalised, with power dispersed. Ajay argues political parties need the same. America's glory years rested on two institutionalised parties with recognisable character, bureaucratic capability and the capacity to nurture ideas. Populism hollows the party out from inside, and the gutting of the Republican Party will matter for the next 25 years.
core_ideas.quote: you also need political parties who are institutionalized, who have dispersion of power, who are not the iron hand of one person or two people.

core_ideas.concept: The Consolidation Playbook
core_ideas.explanation: Müller describes three things populists do once in power. They colonise the state, placing loyalists in independent institutions and discrediting the rest, sometimes by brute force and sometimes slowly. They practise mass clientelism: cronyism, contracts, and protection from especially foreign competition. And they shut down dissent in civil society, with NGOs among the first targets. Ajay links this to China, where the Communist Party has a cell inside every company.
core_ideas.quote: Now you need a completely separate playbook, or an additional playbook, rather, when you get to power to consolidate that power and make sure you don't lose it.

core_ideas.concept: The Chilling Effect
core_ideas.explanation: Regimes don't need to jail everyone. Make an example of a couple of people and everyone else starts self-censoring. Over time people stop noticing their own silence, which makes this kind of repression invisible and hard to call out.
core_ideas.quote: They don't even realize why they are silent. They may not even think they're silent.

core_ideas.concept: Bread and Circus
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay borrows the Roman phrase. 'Bread' is subsidies and transfers that placate the people; he calls one subsidy programme after another a crude form of clientelism that has become normalised. 'Circus' was gladiators in the Colosseum; today it is the drumbeat of noise on TV and social media that stops people thinking about real issues.
core_ideas.quote: So bread and circus is the machinery of the modern populist.

core_ideas.concept: A Fair Election Is More Than a Fair Count
core_ideas.explanation: Votes being counted correctly is not enough. The opposition must be free to fundraise, have advisors, use a free press, organise without coercion and rally in the streets. The right question is how many percentage points state pressure on the opposition shifted the vote. Ajay calibrates with Freedom House: Hungary scores 65/100 yet has effectively lost democracy, so even a respectable-looking score can hide its sustained loss.
core_ideas.quote: An election is only fair and free if rival opposition parties are able to fundraise, are able to have advisors openly talking about them, participating in them, are able to have a free press that will speak openly about what various political parties are saying

core_ideas.concept: Democracy Needs a Republic and a Healthy Discourse
core_ideas.explanation: Power in the people's hands is good. But it needs a republic, with a constitution and safeguards that protect individual rights and constrain the state, and a public discourse where simplistic narratives don't win. Amit says the weak discourse is partly the failure of people like them, who must wade into the mess instead of just complaining.
core_ideas.quote: the people having the power is a damn good thing. That's the whole idea of a democracy. But what you need is two other things.

core_ideas.concept: Eternal Vigilance
core_ideas.explanation: Hungary shows that even in the heart of Europe, liberal values can collapse completely. Amit invokes Jefferson's 'eternal vigilance': civilisation and liberalism are never permanently achieved. Without constant defence, our baser instincts take over.
core_ideas.quote: Every generation has to fight its own battles.

core_ideas.concept: Social Media Pulls Toward the Extremes
core_ideas.explanation: On social media, people join ideological tribes, and status within them comes from signalling, attacking the other side and cancelling insufficiently pure insiders. A vocal minority drags discourse to the extremes even if the silent majority is moderate. Kuran-style preference cascades get amplified. The median voter theorem predicted near-identical centrist candidates (Jeb Bush vs Hillary Clinton), but Trump broke it and won.
core_ideas.quote: when I think of the incentives of social media, I think the incentive everywhere is towards the extremes.

core_ideas.concept: Wokeism Begins Where Liberalism Ends
core_ideas.explanation: Liberalism is about individual freedom, rights and the autonomy of each person, who 'contains multitudes'. Amit sees wokeism as thinking only in groups. It imposes an identity with a ready-made narrative of victimhood or oppression, a version of old class warfare. Amit worries we are left with a contest between left and right populisms, both of which led to disaster in the 20th century.
core_ideas.quote: wokeism begins where liberalism ends.

core_ideas.concept: The Vulgar Familiarity of Social Media Knowledge
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues social media creates a counterfeit of knowledge: 140 characters make people cocky, and clueless people confidently mouth 'truths' at the dinner table. In his father's world, people spoke with care and nuance and would humbly say, 'I have only read four books on this subject.' He sees no easy way out except our own striving.
core_ideas.quote: social media creates a vulgar familiarity

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay, after Amit's point on conspiracy theories: 'Religion is the opiate of the masses. Conspiracy theories are the opiate of the asses.'

Amit the writing teacher polices Ajay's mixed metaphors all episode. First: 'You can pour salt on a wound and you can pour oil on a fire. Why would you pour salt on a fire, Ajay Shah?' ('My mistake.'). Then 'a black eye in the heart of Europe. What is this?' Finally, 'the spinal cord of the foundation. My brain is going to hell,' and the two settle on calling it 'the structural engineering of this episode.'

On Trump's junk-food photo ops, Amit: 'I can completely understand why someone says a hamburger is tasty. Yes, some hamburgers are tasty. But if you tell me a hamburger is good for you, you know, there's a serious kind of problem with that.'
Ajay, deliberately: 'Gentle reader, you will be noticing my explicit use of the word elite, because I want to torment the wokes in the audience as well.'

When Ajay says even star pupil Poland collapsed into populism, Amit coins a 'T-shirt line': 'You are my Poland.' He imagines the genteel, nuanced Ajay suddenly 'burning trucks and beating people up,' with hope that he too can be brought back.
Ajay asks listeners to correct him where he's wrong. Amit: 'They'll correct you if you're right also.' Ajay: 'Please correct me if you think I'm right.'
Amit's 90s nostalgia: downloading photographs over dial-up 'of Samantha Fox or otherwise' and watching them sharpen from pixels. 'Whatever the objectives, you get a thrill.'

Ajay sets up his recommendation with Beauty and the Beast: the male character ('conservative, toxic masculinity, all that stuff') flips through Belle's book and complains there are no pictures. Hence the illustrated On Tyranny, 'that you should give every WhatsApp uncle in your life.'

The episode opens with Amit holding a prop: 'an ancient manuscript that we have found, which looks like a leaf' covered in 'mysterious words in a mysterious language.' Later, when Ajay says events in faraway countries matter to all of us, Amit brings the leaf back with a play on 'for whom the bell tolls': 'not for whom the leaf turns, the leaf turns for thee.'
Ajay pivots to defining populism with the Bee Gees' 'Words': 'It's only words and words are all we have.' Amit: 'I never thought you're gonna quote the Bee Gees at me, but well done.'
Asked what is driving today's polarisation, Ajay quotes 'a poet': 'somebody shout, somebody scream, what happened to the post-war dream?' His answer to the lyric's question is social media.

The frog in slowly boiling water: Amit uses the parable for gradual institutional capture, then debunks it. 'It's a myth. If you heat the water and a frog is in it, the frog will at some point jump out. But it's a great metaphor.'

Ajay traces the mass-media path for simplistic messages: Plato's Republic was already clear-eyed about democracy, then came Mussolini using radio, Hitler organising large-scale rallies, then television, social media and the internet.
'History may not repeat, but it rhymes.' Amit invokes the line to ask what is genuinely new this time, and answers: the pace of technology and the incentives of social media.
Lech Walesa organising the port workers of Poland: Ajay's shorthand for Poland being among the first to build an anti-communist movement before 1989.
'It's the country of John von Neumann.' Ajay on why the world expected great things from post-communist Hungary.
